transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello Dr. Smith. Thank you for fitting me in. I... goodness, where to start? I came in because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore, and it's reached a point where I just don't know what to do with myself. 

If you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table, you would probably be appalled. You can't even see the wood grain anymore. It is completely covered—just mountains of things. It's all my husband’s appointment papers, for one. He has the cardiologist and the eye doctor, and they always hand you those thick after-visit summaries, and I bring them home and set them down meaning to file them, but they just pile up. And mixed right in with his medical papers are all my church flyers. I try to stay involved, you know, with the committees and such, so there are bulletins and schedules everywhere. And then there are the notes and newsletters from the senior center, and just... dozens of these little half-finished lists I make for myself. I write things down on the backs of envelopes to try and get organized, but then I lose the envelope under a flyer, so I have to start a completely new list. 

And the truly terrible part, the reason I'm here, is that I will make myself a cup of tea in the morning, sit down at that table, and I just look at it all. I look at the doctor's note, and then the church flyer, and my brain just sort of freezes. I sit there not knowing which single thing to pick up or do first. I just shuffle the papers around, getting absolutely nowhere, feeling completely overwhelmed, and then suddenly I look up at the clock on the stove and it's four in the afternoon. The whole entire day is just gone. Just vanished! And I haven't accomplished a single thing. It’s been happening every day, and I'm just so exhausted from sitting there doing nothing.
Has this difficulty with organizing your tasks and staying focused on your goals been a lifelong struggle for you, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?

Oh, goodness, no, it's definitely not a new thing. It feels so much heavier now, of course, with just the sheer volume of everything, but if I really sit and think about it... it’s been my whole life. 

I remember years ago, my mother kept all my old report cards in this beautiful cedar chest at the foot of her bed—she was so wonderfully organized, bless her heart, I really don't know why I didn't inherit a single ounce of that from her—but I was looking through those old report cards once, and it was the same story year after year. Even when I was just a little girl in grade school, every single one of my teachers wrote practically the exact same thing. They would always say that I was a very bright girl, but just so careless. Always that word, "careless." 

I was constantly leaving my schoolbooks at home on the kitchen counter, or—and this used to drive my mother absolutely up the wall—I would actually do my homework, sit there at the table and finish it, and then completely forget to take it with me to school. I'd just leave it sitting right there. And during class, oh my, the teachers always had to stand over my shoulder and remind me to finish my seatwork. I'd be looking at the paper, and then I'd be looking out the window at a bird, or just daydreaming, and all the other children would be finishing up and lining up at the door to go outside for recess. The teacher would always have to come over, tap on my desk, and tell me I needed to finish my work before I could go outside and play with the others. 

So, yes, that tendency to just drift off and lose track of what I'm supposed to be doing, it’s always been there. It’s just that back then, I had my mother to pack my schoolbag, and the teachers to tap my desk and keep me moving. And then for years my husband handled a lot of the household organizing before his health declined. Now it's just me trying to manage it all, and I just can't. But those old report cards... they really did paint a picture, didn't they? I used to feel so awful reading them, wondering why I couldn't just be careful like the other girls.

Looking back at those childhood years, besides the daydreaming and forgetting your work, were you also a child who felt like you were constantly 'on the go' or had a hard time staying seated when you were expected to?

Oh, "on the go"... well, goodness, when I was a little girl, girls were really expected to sit quietly like young ladies, so I don't remember running around the classroom like some of the rambunctious little boys did. But the staying seated part... you know, it's funny you ask about that, because that is something I struggle with terribly right now. I don't know if it started back then, but it is certainly happening these days. 

For instance, when I go to my volunteer meetings—the church committees I was telling you about earlier—I just cannot seem to stay in my chair. We have these lovely ladies in the auxiliary, and we'll be right in the middle of discussing the bake sale or the charity drive, and I know, I absolutely know I am supposed to just stay seated and listen to whoever has the floor. But I'll suddenly think of a date, and I just stand up. I'll get up to check the big calendar on the wall, or I'll remember a flyer and get up to look for a paper on the back table, or I'll decide right that very second that I need to refill my water glass. I just keep getting up! 

And it’s not just at the meetings, either. It happens right in my own home, even at supper. My husband and I will sit down to eat, and he'll be trying to tell me about his day or his cardiologist appointment, and I just keep popping up from the table. I'll get up to check the stove, or grab a different spoon, or just... move around the kitchen for no real reason at all. He gets so frustrated with me, bless his heart. He'll say, "Can't you just sit and eat your meal with me for five minutes?" And I want to, I really do, but I just feel this urge to get up and do something, even when I know I should be sitting still and listening to him. It's like my body just decides it's time to stand up and flutter around before my brain can tell it no. So I suppose, even if I wasn't climbing the walls as a child, staying seated is practically impossible for me now. I just always seem to be up and out of my chair before I even realize I've done it.

Looking back at your childhood, before you were expected to sit like a 'young lady,' do you recall having a hard time staying in your seat or feeling the need to be constantly moving during your primary school years?

Well, let me really think back on that... primary school... we were at the old brick schoolhouse on Elm Street. I can still picture the classroom so clearly, with those heavy wooden desks, you know the ones that had the little inkwells in the top right corner even though we didn't use them anymore? And the seats were attached right to the desk behind you. 

But as for having a hard time staying in my seat, or feeling like I needed to be constantly moving around... no, I really don't think so. I don't remember feeling restless in my body back then at all. Like I was saying before, I was always just staring out the window at the birds, or tracing the wood grain on my desk with my pencil. Mrs. Gable—she was my second-grade teacher, a lovely woman but very strict, always wore these stiff collared blouses with a little cameo pin—she never, ever had to tell me to sit down. She had to tell me to pay attention, yes, or to finish my arithmetic, but never to take my seat. 

There was a boy in that class, Tommy Peterson I think his name was, who was always popping out of his seat to sharpen his pencil or pull the girls' pigtails, and I remember just watching him and wondering why on earth he couldn't just sit still. Isn't that just the most ironic thing? Because now I'm the one who can't sit still at the supper table! But back then, when I was little, no, I was perfectly content to just sit there in my little wooden chair for hours on end. I wasn't squirming or feeling like I had a motor running inside me or anything like that. I was just lost in my own little world, quiet as a mouse. 

My mother used to say I was her easiest child to take to Sunday service because I would just sit in the pew like a little statue. My mind would be a million miles away, of course, thinking about what we were having for Sunday dinner or making up stories about the people in the stained glass windows, but my body... no, my body was perfectly still. It's just so strange how things change, isn't it?

When you find yourself getting up from your seat during meals or meetings, does it feel like you are being driven by an internal sense of restlessness or a physical 'motor' that makes it hard to stay still, or are you usually getting up because you are distracted by something else you suddenly remembered you needed to do?

A motor? Oh, my, no, I wouldn't say it feels like a motor at all. It’s not a physical feeling in my body, like my legs are twitching or I have this bursting need to go run a mile. I don't feel jittery or... or restless in my bones, if that makes sense. It’s definitely the other thing you said. It’s the distractions. It’s always a sudden thought that just pops into my head out of nowhere, and before I even have a chance to reason with myself, I’m already on my feet. 

Like, just the other evening—this is a perfect example—we were having a lovely pot roast for supper. I make it with those little pearl onions Arthur loves so much, even though they are just a dreadful pain to peel because you have to blanch them in boiling water first and then pinch the little ends off so they slip out of their skins—but anyway, we were sitting right there at the table. He was telling me all about his brother's new golf cart, and suddenly, clear as a bell, I remembered that I hadn't moved the wet towels from the washing machine into the dryer. Now, the laundry room is all the way down the hall, past the guest bathroom, but the thought just completely hijacked my brain. I thought, 'Oh no, the towels are going to sit there and get that awful mildew smell,' and up I went! 

I didn't feel physically restless at all, I just... I felt like I had to go take care of the towels right that very second, because I knew if I didn't, I would completely forget them again until the next morning. And poor Arthur, he was right in the middle of a sentence about the battery life on that silly golf cart, and there I was, halfway to the hallway with my dinner napkin still clutched in my hand. 

So, yes, it’s always something like that. It’s remembering a flyer at the church meeting, or the laundry, or suddenly wondering if I locked the back porch door because Mrs. Higgins down the street had someone steal her garden hose last week and you just can't be too careful these days. It's never my body needing to move, it's just my mind pulling me away to something else I forgot to do, and my body just sort of follows along without my permission.
